text: Value iteration, from the last lesson, needs a map of the world: the probability of every transition. Usually an agent has no such map; a robot does not know in advance where a slippery floor will send it. Q-learning, introduced by Chris Watkins in nineteen eighty-nine, learns to act well from experience alone.

Instead of valuing states, Q-learning values state and action pairs. Q of s and a is the return you expect if you take action a in state s, and act optimally afterwards. Once you know Q, choosing is easy: in each state, pick the action with the largest Q, without needing any model of where the actions lead.

The agent keeps a table of Q values, starting at zero. After each step it holds a small piece of evidence: it was in state s, took action a, received reward r, and landed in a new state. The target is r plus gamma times the best Q value available in the new state, and the agent moves its old estimate a fraction alpha, the learning rate, toward that target. This is called temporal difference learning: correcting one guess with the next guess, like updating your expected arrival time at every station rather than waiting until the journey ends.

Notice the max in the target. It means Q-learning learns about the best policy even while it behaves differently, which is called off-policy learning. That freedom matters, because the agent has to explore. A common rule is epsilon-greedy: usually take the best-looking action, but with a small probability epsilon, pick one at random, so that untried actions still get a chance to prove themselves.

Watkins and Dayan proved that in a finite problem, if every state and action keeps being tried and the learning rate shrinks in the right way, the table converges to the optimal Q values. In a small grid you can watch it happen: early episodes wander, and value spreads backwards from the goal, one step at a time, as each discovery is passed on to the states that lead to it.

A table cannot cover every screen of a video game. In twenty fifteen, Mnih and colleagues at DeepMind replaced the table with a neural network, the deep Q-network, and trained it to play Atari games from raw pixels, reaching a level comparable to a professional human tester on many of the forty-nine games they tried. Two tricks kept training stable: a replay buffer that reuses shuffled past experience, and a slowly updated copy of the network that supplies the targets.

Q-learning learns values and derives its actions from them. For a language model, with an enormous number of possible tokens at every step, it is often easier to adjust the policy directly, and that is the subject of the next lesson: policy gradients.
